post.title: Retrace: Local-First Screen Memory for macOS and Your Agents
post.description: How I forked retrace into agent-first, local-only screen memory for macOS: Apple Vision OCR, SQLite/FTS5 search, and a privacy-gated CLI for agents.
post.excerpt: Everything you see on screen disappears the moment it scrolls away, and your coding agents leave no record at all. Retrace Agentfirst captures, OCRs, and indexes your Mac screen entirely locally, then hands that memory to agents through a bounded, read-only CLI.
post.content:
My screen is the highest-bandwidth log of my work, and until recently it was write-only. I saw a PR comment three days ago and cannot find it now. An error message flashed past in a terminal that is long gone. Browser history does not cover it. File search does not either. Nothing indexes what was visibly on my screen.

There is a newer version of the same problem. My machine is not just mine anymore: Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor sessions run on it all day. Nobody has a record of what the agents did, which project the work belonged to, or how to hand yesterday's context back to today's agent. Not without shipping private screen data to a cloud service, anyway.

The README frames it as four questions. What did I do? What did my agents do? Which project was that work for? Can I find, summarize, and reuse the context later, locally?

**Retrace Agentfirst** is my answer. It is a local-first macOS app that continuously captures your screen, OCRs everything with Apple Vision into a searchable SQLite index, and exposes that memory to coding agents through a bounded, privacy-gated CLI, plus daily markdown journals written by a local Ollama model.

## Credit where it belongs

Attribution first. This is a fork of [haseab/retrace](https://github.com/haseab/retrace) (MIT), itself inspired by Rewind AI. The heavy lifting is upstream work by @haseab: the capture pipeline, the OCR, the FTS5 search, the timeline UI, the HEVC storage, the Rewind import. What my fork adds is the agent layer: a read-only `retrace-cli`, bounded context queries, local journal generation, a written product constitution, per-module docs aimed at coding agents, and a monochrome Notion/Linear-style UI direction.

The fork also keeps a testable compatibility promise: after any upstream merge, upstream Retrace must still be able to open the same database and videos. The app bundle is rebranded to `io.retrace.agentfirst`, but storage and keychain deliberately stay on upstream's `io.retrace.app`.

## Getting it running

The only real install path today is building from source on macOS 13 or newer. The README has a curl one-liner and the repo carries a Homebrew cask, but both are templates with placeholder URLs. There are zero published releases. Build it yourself:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/aryateja2106/retrace-agentfirst.git
cd retrace-agentfirst
swift build
```

That builds the whole SwiftPM package: app, CLI, and helpers. If you only want the agent CLI:

```bash
swift build --product retrace-cli
```

Sanity-check the binary:

```bash
.build/debug/retrace-cli --help
```

The help text states the privacy posture in plain words: "No localhost API or MCP server is started. Read commands use a read-only SQLite connection."

## How it works

1. **Capture.** A Swift actor in `Capture/CaptureManager.swift` coordinates continuous capture through a CoreGraphics CGWindowList backend. Frames are taken every 2 seconds by default, plus on window changes and mouse clicks, then run through pixel-based deduplication. Each frame is tagged with the app bundle ID, window name, and browser URL. Privacy filters (excluded apps, private-window detection) run before anything is persisted.
2. **Storage.** Instead of millions of screenshots, frames are packed into HEVC video segments by a hardware-accelerated AVAssetWriter/VideoToolbox encoder. Same trick Rewind AI used, here fully open source.
3. **OCR.** Apple's Vision framework (`VNRecognizeTextRequest` in accurate mode) extracts text from every frame, entirely on-device.
4. **Index.** Sanitized text lands in `retrace.db` under `~/Library/Application Support/Retrace/` with an FTS5 full-text index, and search uses bm25 ranking. A fun detail: the Database module links SQLCipher even though Retrace's own database is unencrypted, because the Rewind import must read Rewind's encrypted database and you cannot mix two SQLite builds in one app.
5. **Surface.** A timeline viewer with frame navigation, search, copy, comments, and `retrace://` deeplinks, plus a dashboard with app usage, screen time, storage, and recording-health metrics. That dashboard is what "time tracking" means today.

## The agent layer

This is the part the fork exists for. `retrace-cli` is a separate SwiftPM executable that opens the same database through a read-only connection factory and exposes deliberately bounded queries. The bounds are enforced in SQL bind parameters, not vibes: every query is clamped to a maximum of 2,000 frames, and per-frame text is clamped between 128 and 12,000 characters. Results come back as JSON with timestamp, app, window, URL, and OCR text. Never screenshots, video files, or raw database paths.

```bash
retrace-cli context recent --hours 1 --json
retrace-cli context search "pull request" --hours 24 --json
```

Consent is an exit code. Every write command (journal generate or append, storage export or adopt) hard-fails with exit code 64 unless you pass `--yes` or `--dry-run`. The confirmation prompt is designed for agents, not humans. An agent that has not been told to write cannot write.

And by hard constraint in `PRODUCT_CONTEXT.md`, there is no always-on localhost API and no MCP server by default. The integration surface is the CLI, full stop.

More commands worth knowing:

```bash
retrace-cli recording status --json
retrace-cli storage inspect --json
retrace-cli storage export --to ~/Retrace-Portable-Export --yes --json
```

The export copies databases, WAL/SHM sidecars, chunk folders, and non-secret settings into a portable folder. It never touches Keychain secrets.

## Journals: your day, summarized locally

Once the screen is indexed, a local model can summarize it. `DailyJournalManager` runs periodically (hourly by default, with a 15-minute minimum cadence) and collects a bounded digest of already-persisted OCR text: at most 120 frames per window, 2,000 characters per frame, 24,000 characters of prompt in total, and only frames at least 180 seconds old. It sends that digest to a local Ollama endpoint at `127.0.0.1:11434` and writes the summary as a markdown file with `privacy: local-only` YAML frontmatter into a folder you choose, which can be an Obsidian vault. The journal layer reads only indexed OCR text. It never decodes screenshots or video.

```bash
retrace-cli ollama status --model gemma4:e4b --json
retrace-cli journal generate --hours 1 --dry-run --json
retrace-cli journal today --json
```

The `gemma4:e4b` string is just the default in code; point `--model` at whatever you have pulled in Ollama. You can also append manual notes:

```bash
echo "shipped the CLI bounds work" | retrace-cli journal append --stdin --yes
```

## Docs written for two audiences

The repo is written for two audiences at once. Humans get the README. Agents get per-module `AGENTS.md` files, a `CLI/SKILL.md` skill file, and a `CLAUDE.md` that is deliberately just a thin compatibility pointer. The product constitution's most interesting clauses are anti-features: no always-on localhost API, no MCP bridge by default, no cloud telemetry, no raw screenshot exposure. Commitments about what the app will refuse to become.

For development: the test suite covers Database, Storage, Capture, Processing, Search, App, and UI targets, plus a concurrency lint required by the regression policy:

```bash
swift test
./scripts/check_no_nanoseconds_sleep.sh
```

## Honest limitations

- **This is an early-stage fork, not a from-scratch product.** The core engine is upstream's. My original contribution is the agent layer, the constitution docs, packaging, and the UI direction. The README itself says "early... expect breaking changes."
- **No binary releases yet.** The DMG, curl, and Homebrew paths are templates. Building from source is the only install path.
- **"Time tracking" currently means dashboard metrics:** screen time and app usage. The fuller calendar and day-timeline tracker with project attribution, and human-versus-agent work separation, are roadmap items, not shipped features.
- **No voice.** whisper.cpp is bundled but deliberately disabled, marked "Release 2 only" in `Package.swift`.
- **Search is FTS5 keyword matching,** not semantic or vector search. That code is excluded from the build.
- **Journal quality depends on Ollama.** You need it running locally with a model pulled.
- **Docs have inconsistencies.** The Capture module README says ScreenCaptureKit, but the wired backend is CGWindowListCapture.
- **No benchmarks.** There are no performance, battery, or accuracy numbers anywhere in the repo, and Vision OCR misses will make some screen text unfindable.

## What's next

The roadmap's next phase is the reason I forked: a real day-timeline time tracker with project attribution, and separating human work from agent work in the same index, so that "what did my agents do yesterday, and for which project?" becomes a query. Audio transcription is slated for Release 2. Release scripts (`create-release.sh`, `create-dmg.sh`) exist to build a signed app and DMG; I have not run them yet, and the first published release is high on the list.

[The code is on GitHub, MIT licensed](https://github.com/aryateja2106/retrace-agentfirst). If you are wiring screen memory into your own agents, I would like to hear what bounds you would set.
